Chapter 3: Patience first

Nina asks a question near the start of her first chapter: “We have read inspiring texts about patience, but do we realize when there is an opportunity to develop it in our daily life?” The journey gave the travellers plenty of opportunities. This chapter looks at what Acharn Sujin taught about patience itself.

The verses. Nina quotes two verses from the Dhammapada (the Buddha’s verses on the teaching), numbers 183 and 184:

“To abstain1 from evil, to cultivate2 wholesomeness3, to purify4 the mind, - this is the teaching of the Buddhas. Forbearing5 patience is the highest ascetism6, nibbāna is the supreme, say the Buddhas; he, verily7 is not a recluse8 who harms another; nor is he an ascetic who oppresses9 others.”

Nibbāna (the end of all troubles) is the goal of the whole teaching, and the verse puts patience right beside it. “It is said that one should abstain from evil, develop wholesomeness and purify the mind. However, we forget that patience is most essential.” And: ““Without patience one cannot attain enlightenment10”, Acharn said.”

Patience comes first. The same teaching is found in the Ovāda Pāṭimokkha (the Exhortation11 to the Pāṭimokkha), which the Buddhas of the past gave to their monks12. There, “the order is different: patience is mentioned first, and this is very appropriate.” Patience is needed before anything else, because developing understanding takes a very long time. “We need great patience to develop understanding of all realities13 of our daily life.”

Patience and loving-kindness. People like the idea of mettā (loving-kindness14). But it “cannot be developed if one does not see the danger of dosa and the benefit of patience”. Dosa (aversion15) is the opposite of patience. A person who does not see that dosa (aversion) is harmful will not see why patience matters.

Not a concept of patience. It is easy to think about patience in a general way, as a fine quality that a person has or lacks. Acharn Sujin brought it down to single moments:

“Acharn showed us very clearly during this journey that at the moment of akusala citta there is impatience and at the moment of kusala citta there is patience.”

patience is not a thing a person owns it is there in every wholesome moment, and gone in every unwholesome one

one moment after another →

akusala kusala akusala akusala kusala kusala

impatience patience impatience impatience patience patience unwholesome wholesome unwholesome unwholesome wholesome wholesome “at the moment of akusala citta there is impatience and at the moment of kusala citta there is patience.”

So patience is not a thing a person owns. It is there whenever the citta (consciousness16) is kusala (wholesome), and gone whenever the citta (consciousness) is akusala (unwholesome17). “When there is awareness18 of akusala we can see that it is ugly and we can understand more clearly its disadvantage19.”

Patience with pleasant things too. Most people think patience is only for unpleasant things. Acharn Sujin said it is needed for pleasant things as well. “When a pleasant object20 presents itself, usually lobha arises21 and in that case there is no patience. When, instead of lobha, kusala citta arises there is patience.” A person who sees a shop full of beautiful things and wants them all has no patience at that moment, though nothing unpleasant is happening.

Levels of awareness. Sati (awareness) has levels. “Awareness is non-forgetfulness of what is wholesome, kusala. Awareness accompanies generosity22, it accompanies kusala citta that is abstaining from ill deeds23, it accompanies each kusala citta.” There is sati (awareness) when someone gives a gift, and when someone holds back an unkind word. Then there is a higher level: “Awareness of the level of satipaṭṭhāna is directly aware of mental24 phenomena25, nāma, and physical phenomena, rūpa, as they appear one at a time through one of the six doors.” Satipaṭṭhāna (direct awareness of realities) is aware of seeing as seeing, of sound as sound, of anger as anger, without a person in it. Its aim “is to see realities as they are: as impermanent26, dukkha (suffering27) and non-self28“.

“Awareness is non-forgetfulness of what is wholesome, kusala.” it accompanies each kusala citta (wholesome consciousness) awareness of the level of satipaṭṭhāna directly aware of nāma and rūpa, one at a time awareness with abstaining when an unkind word is held back awareness with generosity when a gift is given

“There can be awareness of realities at different levels.”

A Journey with Dhamma for Young Readers  ·  17

Page 17
Journey Chapter 3: Patience first (p. 16–30) p. 18

Gabi and the crying baby. Gabi told Acharn Sujin that she was not yet directly aware of nāma (mind) and rūpa (matter29), but that she could be aware of akusala citta (unwholesome consciousness) in her daily life:

“She reads Jātakas (the Buddha’s Birth stories) and she finds that she often is in the same situation as described in the Jātakas. She read in a Jātaka story that one should not speak when one is angry and she could apply this in her daily life. When someone’s baby was crying she understood the ugliness of aversion and that was a condition30 for kusala citta: she would not say anything about the baby’s crying.”

“When someone's baby was crying she understood the ugliness of aversion and that was a condition for kusala citta: she would not say anything about the baby's crying.”

Acharn Sujin’s answer was short: “This shows progress in the development of right understanding”. Nobody can expect many moments of satipaṭṭhāna (direct awareness of realities), “but awareness of other levels can arise”. Even the Buddha, in the lives before he became the Buddha, “developed the perfections31 (pāramīs) with awareness and right understanding of different levels”. Nina writes: “We found it very encouraging to hear this.”

All kinds of kusala. Acharn Sujin had said many times “that all kinds of kusala should be cultivated so that sati and the other sobhana cetasikas (beautiful mental factors32) can develop”. Each kusala citta (wholesome consciousness) adds to the conditions for understanding. She also warned against a trap. A person may be “merely thinking of the Dhamma” and never notice the akusala cetasikas (unwholesome mental factors) that arise all day. “Acharn said that people want to have great patience, but forget to develop patience at this moment.”

Look at akusala as akusala. Nina ends with the Buddha’s words from the Itivuttaka (As It Was Said):

A Journey with Dhamma for Young Readers  ·  18

Page 18
Journey Chapter 3: Patience first (p. 16–30) p. 19

“‘Look at akusala as akusala’ is the first dhamma-teaching. ‘Seeing akusala as akusala, be disgusted with it, be cleansed33 of it, be freed of it’ is the second dhamma-teaching.”

First see the unwholesome for what it is. Then turn away from it. The next chapter shows how that happened: at the tombs of the kings, in the bus, at Cairo airport, and in a hotel room after one o’clock at night, waiting for suitcases.

Chapter 4: Tired, hungry and waiting

“Usually akusala citta with aversion arises when we feel tired.”

“Do you like it to be tired?” “While we walked around the tombs of the Egyptian kings, or while we had to sit for a long time in the bus or at the airport we became tired.” Alan wondered whether tiredness is in the body or in the mind. Acharn Sujin did not answer with a theory. “Acharn asked him, “Do you like it to be tired?” Alan answered that he did not like it and then it became clear that he had aversion1.” The tiredness itself was one thing. The not liking it was another: a moment of dosa (aversion), which is akusala (unwholesome2).

Most people treat tiredness as a good excuse. “We use tiredness as an excuse not to develop kusala at such a moment but, Acharn said, it is no excuse.” Nina gives more examples from the journey:

“When we have to wait a long time for dinner and we become faint with hunger, or the shower in the hotel room does not work, we can ask ourselves, “Do we like this?” Then we can know how much aversion we have; we begin to see akusala as akusala and to understand its disadvantage3.”

A Journey with Dhamma for Young Readers  ·  20

Page 20
Journey Chapter 3: Patience first (p. 16–30) p. 21

tired at the tombs of the kings aversion is seen faint with hunger, waiting for dinner dosa (aversion), akusala “Do we like this?” (unwholesome) the question to ask “we begin to see akusala the shower in the hotel does not work as akusala”

the luggage does not come the tiredness or hunger is one thing; the not liking it is another “Then we can know how much aversion we have; we begin to see akusala as akusala and to understand its disadvantage.”

The question “Do we like this?” does not mend the shower. It shows the aversion hiding behind the hunger. “When we give in to aversion we only think of ourselves. Whereas when we think of others kusala citta with patience arises4.”

Nina’s disappointment. Nina had come on the journey for the Dhamma talks, and sometimes there was no time for them. “There was not always an opportunity for Dhamma discussions during this journey and then I was disappointed.” Acharn Sujin’s reply is one of the longest speeches in the book. Here is part of it:

“When aversion arises it is evident that it is caused by something you want to have but which you do not obtain. We should trace the cause of aversion, otherwise we cannot get rid of the cause. You cling5 to the time for dinner or breakfast. You cling to Dhamma talk. Everything is dhamma, and it depends on your considering and understanding whether you can see this.”

Even wanting a Dhamma talk is clinging. Acharn went on: “Be patient, receive all kinds of vipākacittas that are conditioned6 by previous kamma. Just let go of the things you are used to or you would like to have.” Whatever arrives through the senses, pleasant or not, is a vipākacitta (result7 consciousness8), to be received. “One can be calm and happy, even when facing difficult situations.”

The lost luggage. The travellers flew back from Turkey to Cairo. At the airport they “had to be patient, waiting for one hour for a piece of luggage which was lost and then found again”. Then, at the hotel, they had to wait in their room for the suitcases until after one o’clock at night. The next day Nina told Acharn Sujin what she had felt.

A Journey with Dhamma for Young Readers  ·  21

Page 21
Journey Chapter 3: Patience first (p. 16–30) p. 22

“Yesterday we had to wait at the airport for the luggage a long time. It was quite a test.”

Nina: “My luggage did not come. Patience has a certain limit, after that there is no more patience.” Acharn: “What is the use of being impatient? Only right understanding can see that it is useless. When there is impatience there is no right understanding which sees the benefit of patience. We need right understanding in any situation.”

Nina tried again: “There can be patience to a certain degree and then one forgets about it.” Acharn answered: “That is why sati is necessary in any situation.” Nina: “Even if you lose your suitcase?” Acharn: “If you see the benefit of higher understanding it is time to develop all kusala dhammas.”

Nina said that moments of impatience are bound to come anyway. Acharn agreed that they come when there are conditions9, “but it depends on the development of paññā whether one continues to accumulate10 more akusala”.

Nina: “I did not realize that the moments of impatience really hinder11 paññā.” Acharn: “Nothing can hinder paññā. However, if you do not understand the disadvantage of akusala you will have more akusala. People desire great paññā, but is there paññā that sees the uselessness of akusala at this moment?”

Nina admitted the small thing she had done at the airport: “When the luggage did not come I was so impatient, I lifted my hands. That was conditioned by impatience. There was no awareness12.” Acharn said that patience shows in body and speech too: “Patience can condition one to refrain13 from speaking certain words or from doing what is akusala.” And she called the long wait a test:

“Yesterday we had to wait at the airport for the luggage a long time. It was quite a test. In this way we can develop more wholesome14 cetasikas. Only reading and writing about the Dhamma is not enough, one should consider precisely the reality15 of this moment.”

A Journey with Dhamma for Young Readers  ·  22

Page 22
Journey Chapter 3: Patience first (p. 16–30) p. 23

Pain. Nina had backache while waiting at the airport. Acharn Sujin said: “If you do not think much of the pain, it does not appear. Other things appear as objects16, such as sound and hearing. One should forget about oneself, otherwise one is self-centered all the time.”

Alan is ill. Just before the flight to Turkey, “Alan was very sick and he did not want to continue traveling. He was afraid of being sick on the plane.” Acharn Sujin said to him:

“Do not think of it, let it go. Everything just arises because of conditions. It is of no use to try to control your body. Awareness is aware naturally, this is the way. Develop understanding at any time, also when you cannot control your stomach.”

Nina adds one sentence: “Alan came along on the plane and he was not sick anymore.”

Parties. The last talk in this part was about Nina’s life at home. She found her social life tiring, “always receiving guests or going out to parties”, and said so, with aversion, every week. Acharn Sujin said: “Sometimes it looks as if you think of yourself first.” Nina agreed: “It is the self that is in the way.” Acharn’s answer turned the whole thing round:

“If you think of making other people happy by entertaining them and going out to their parties, you will have the energy17 to do this, instead of thinking that it is too much. You can think: ‘It is my time to help’, and then kusala citta can arise. Everything can be changed by right understanding.”

The guests were the same guests. What changed was the citta (consciousness): from thinking that it is too much to thinking “It is my time to help”.

Chapter 5: This moment

“In Egypt and Turkey we saw golden treasures, jewelry and objects decorated with glittering precious stones, which have been collected in olden times and are unique in the world.”

Golden treasures. “In Egypt and Turkey we saw golden treasures, jewelry and objects1 decorated with glittering precious stones, which have been collected in olden times and are unique in the world.” The travellers stood in front of museum cases and looked at every detail. Nina noticed what the looking did to the mind: “Most of the time clinging2 arises3 after seeing, and when we are absorbed in the details of what we see our clinging becomes more obvious.” The seeing lasts a moment. What comes after it is saññā (remembrance4), which “remembers what is seen and cittas think of it for a long time”.

Whenever a person is not giving, or keeping good conduct, or developing the mind, the citta (consciousness5) is akusala (unwholesome6): “Even when we believe that our thinking is harmless the citta is likely to be akusala citta. We often think with akusala citta about people.”

“Where is that being?” Acharn Sujin said:

“Where is that being? It is only a story in your mind. Previous experiences7 condition8 the thought of a being9. Gradually we can come to understand what is meant by “being alone” with visible object at the moment of seeing, because there is nobody in the visible object. One can be alone at the moment of hearing sound, because there is no idea of anyone at that moment.”

What is seen is colour. The person is thought of afterwards, from memory. “We should often consider that we see visible object, no husband or wife, friend or relative.”

Lodewijk. Acharn Sujin used Nina’s own husband as the example. “Acharn said to me: “You assume that there is Lodewijk, but you just enjoy paññatti, a concept10. What is more beneficial11: understanding that there is a reality12, not Lodewijk, or thinking that he is Lodewijk?”” A paññatti (concept) is an idea put

A Journey with Dhamma for Young Readers  ·  26

Page 26
Journey Chapter 3: Patience first (p. 16–30) p. 27

together by thinking. Nobody told Nina not to love her husband. Acharn asked only what was more beneficial to understand.

Death. Nina asked what she could do if her husband died. Acharn Sujin said: “When he dies and you would feel lonely, you cling to just air, to nothing. Where is he after death? You cling to your own memory. We should often consider this.” Nina said that one has to be prepared. “When I said that we have to be prepared, she said: “Now you are preparing.”” There is no other time to prepare than now. “We can only prepare ourselves for a great loss by understanding the present moment more clearly.”

This moment. Acharn Sujin said it in many ways. “We should not worry about enlightenment13, but what about the understanding of this moment? Understanding can develop from one moment to a following moment. There is no other way but the understanding of the reality of this moment.” Once she was yawning, and Nina asked whether she was tired. The answer was: “It is just this moment.”

Thinking. Nina wondered whether paying less attention to details would help her to know what seeing is. Acharn answered:

“You do not have to try to prevent thinking. When thinking thinks a great deal, it is time to understand thinking. Develop understanding now, that is better than waiting to see the precise distinction between nāma and rūpa, or the rapidity14 of their arising and falling away15. That is beyond our understanding at this moment. One studies in order to have more understanding of realities, we have to go stage by stage. There should be no expectation of result16.”

Nobody has to stop thinking. Thinking is a nāma (mind) like any other, and when it is going on, it is the reality to be understood.

The actors on the stage. Seeing happens in a short process17 of cittas (moments of consciousness) through the eye-door; hearing in another process through the ear-door; thinking through the mind-door. In between the processes come bhavaṅga-cittas (life-continuum18 consciousness), which do not experience the sights and sounds of the world at all. “When we are fast asleep and not dreaming, bhavanga-cittas arise and fall away, succeeding19 one another.” Acharn Sujin compared it all to a play:

“The cittas experiencing the sense objects are the actors and the bhavanga-cittas in between processes are like the darkness in between the acts, when the curtain is drawn. Each time when the curtain opens there is a new act going to be played. One never knows beforehand what kind of act will be played, it is a surprise. The acts change with great rapidity: seeing arises, then hearing, then thinking. They seem to occur all at the same time, but in reality there are different “acts” separated by bhavanga-cittas. They have no connection with each other.”

seeing hearing thinking seeing curtain curtain curtain an act an act an act an act the dark gaps are bhavaṅga-cittas (life-continuum): the curtain is drawn, and the next act is a surprise “The cittas experiencing the sense objects are the actors and the bhavanga-cittas in between processes are like the darkness in between the acts, when the curtain is drawn.”

Nina adds: “Each act is so short, it is already over before we realize it. This reminds us that there is no self who could direct the drama of life.”

“Each time when the curtain opens there is a new act going to be played.”

Praise. Acharn Sujin spoke about praise and honour:

“One may cling to praise and fame, but that is very dangerous. People become infatuated20 with these insignificant21 things. Praise is called an axe that falls from heaven. It wounds if one does not know how to receive it. We should learn to receive both blame and praise. We should get rid of the idea of rank, it destroys kusala. It is more beneficial to be “nobody”; to get rid of the idea of my body, of the idea of self, of rank or praise.”

A Journey with Dhamma for Young Readers  ·  28

Page 28
Journey Chapter 3: Patience first (p. 16–30) p. 29

Praise, she said, is “only words people will forget immediately after they have been spoken. The person who clings to praise wants more.” The lesson is the same as in the museum: “We attach great importance to what we experience, but it only lasts for a moment.”

Chapter 6: The perfections on the road

Ten good qualities. “We have to continue to develop right understanding and all the wholesome1 qualities which are the “perfections2”, pāramīs.” The pāramīs (perfections) are the ten qualities that the Buddha developed in the lives before his last one, when he was still the Bodhisatta, the being on the way to becoming a Buddha. Nina lists them: “generosity3, morality4, renunciation5, wisdom, energy6, patience, truthfulness7, determination8, loving-kindness9 and equanimity10.” Everyone else needs them too: “We also should develop the perfections together with satipaṭṭhāna so that eventually enlightenment11 can be attained.”

the ten pāramīs (perfections) the Bodhisatta developed

dāna sīla nekkhamma paññā viriya generosity morality renunciation wisdom energy

khanti sacca adhiṭṭhāna mettā upekkhā patience truthfulness determination loving-kindness equanimity

“Patience is indispensable with the development of all the perfections.”

“generosity, morality, renunciation, wisdom, energy, patience, truthfulness, determination, loving-kindness and equanimity.”

No hurry. The travellers asked which perfections a person should develop most. Acharn Sujin’s answers took away the hurry: “one should not expect it to be fully developed tonight or tomorrow. Is the development of understanding at this moment not enough? We should let go of all expectations.” And about choosing: “It seems that ‘we’ can develop them, but it depends on conditions12 which type of kusala arises13 at a particular moment. When we learn about the ten perfections we are encouraged to develop all of them.”

Loving-kindness. People read about boundless mettā (loving-kindness) and think about it. Acharn Sujin said something more down to earth: “My goal is not infinite mettā, but to extend mettā to different people at any time, and not to particular people.” Nina writes: “This reminded us again that the perfections should be developed naturally, when the opportunity arises, and that this is different from mere thinking about them.”

Patience and aeons. “When we see the extent of our defilements14 more clearly we can understand that it takes a long time, even innumerable15 lives, to eradicate16 them. It should not disturb us that we cannot attain enlightenment soon, that it takes aeons17.” Gabi had a short way of saying it: “Thinking of aeons will make patience grow.”

Morality. Sīla (morality) is one of the perfections. Acharn Sujin said that abstention18 can act fast: “the cetasika that is abstention can stop angry words, even if one has opened one’s mouth already”. Nina confessed that she complained to her husband when she was tired or hungry. Acharn answered:
